pharm: Oral non-opioid cough suppressant chemically related to the ester local anesthetics (e.g., tetracaine); it anesthetizes the stretch (pulmonary) receptors of the vagal afferents in the respiratory passages, lungs, and pleura, reducing the cough reflex at its source without depressing the respiratory center.

summary: Benzonatate is a non-narcotic oral antitussive used for the symptomatic relief of cough in adults and children over 10 years of age. Structurally related to the ester local anesthetics, it suppresses cough by anesthetizing the stretch receptors in the airways, lungs, and pleura. The usual dose is one 100 mg or 200 mg capsule three times daily, up to 600 mg/day. Capsules must be swallowed whole - they must never be broken, chewed, dissolved, cut, or crushed, because release of benzonatate in the mouth causes local anesthesia and choking/laryngospasm. Accidental ingestion, especially in children under 10, can be rapidly fatal (within an hour), and intentional overdose has caused death; the product must be kept out of the reach of children.
indications: Symptomatic relief of cough in patients older than 10 years of age

moa: Benzonatate is a peripherally acting non-narcotic antitussive structurally related to the ester-type local anesthetics (such as tetracaine and procaine). It acts by anesthetizing the stretch (pulmonary) receptors located in the respiratory passages, lungs, and pleura that are stimulated during the act of breathing and trigger the cough reflex via the vagus nerve. By dampening the activity of these peripheral sensory receptors, benzonatate reduces the cough reflex at its source. It exerts no analgesic central action and does not inhibit the respiratory center at recommended doses, distinguishing it from opioid antitussives.

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of benzonatate in pregnant women. It should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether benzonatate is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants and limited data, caution should be exercised; avoid use during breastfeeding where possible.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is described in the labeling. Use with general caution in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is described in the labeling. Use with caution in patients with hepatic impairment.

missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember if you still need it for cough. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose - do not take two doses at once. Take only as needed and do not exceed the maximum daily dose.
overdose: Overdose can be rapidly fatal. Onset of symptoms may occur within about an hour; ingestion of even one or two capsules by a young child can be lethal. Features include restlessness, tremors, CNS stimulation followed by depression, convulsions, deep unconsciousness, and cardiac arrest; chewing the capsule causes acute oropharyngeal anesthesia and airway compromise. There is no specific antidote - treatment is immediate gastric decontamination as appropriate, airway protection, anticonvulsants for seizures, and intensive supportive/cardiorespiratory care.
